1.4 Configuration

The default config is ~/.config/diskproxy/config.json. A general example:

{
  "source": "/absolute/path/to/folder",
  "plugin": "passthrough",
  "mode": "disk",
  "label": "DiskProxy",
  "port": 0,
  "plugins": {}
}
Key Meaning Default
source Folder to present; a path given to start overrides it none, required
plugin passthrough, pmp or previews passthrough
mode disk, nfs or webdav disk
label Volume name, up to 11 UTF-16 code units plugin’s default
writable Disk mode only: mount through a shadow file and capture writes false
mountpoint NFS mode only: where to mount ~/Volumes/LABEL
port Localhost port; 0 picks a free one 0
plugins.<name> Settings for that plugin {}

Paths in a config file are taken literally: write absolute paths, not ~. Unknown keys are errors, so a misspelling is reported rather than ignored.

Settings are applied in this order, later ones winning: the config file, then --set KEY=VALUE, then explicit flags such as --label. --set parses its value as JSON when it can, otherwise as a string, and reaches into plugin settings with dotted keys:

diskproxy start --set plugins.pmp.hide_ingested=true
diskproxy start --set 'plugins.previews.ratings="/absolute/path/to/ratings"'

The launcher reads mode from the config file to decide how to mount, so put "mode": "nfs" in the file rather than passing it with --set. The launcher refuses --mode, --check and --register; those belong to diskproxy-server.

1.4.1 Checking a config without serving

diskproxy-server --config ~/views/library.json --check

This validates the config and the plugin settings, prepares the plugin, prints its startup information as JSON and exits, without mounting or registering anything.
